","width":1012,"height":796,"source":"Figure excerpt cropped from user-supplied Biological Psychology, 14th ed., PDF","cropPdfPoints":[70,330,576,728],"status":"figure number and printed source page verified against original PDF"},{"id":"figure-1-24","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h07","number":"1.24","title":"Propagation of an action potential","printedPage":31,"pdfPage":49,"alt":"Three successive diagrams showing action-potential propagation along the axon membrane and movement of ions.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":1012,"height":1200,"source":"Figure excerpt cropped from user-supplied Biological Psychology, 14th ed., PDF","cropPdfPoints":[70,70,576,670],"status":"figure number and printed source page verified against original PDF"},{"id":"figure-1-26","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h09","number":"1.26","title":"Saltatory conduction in a myelinated axon","printedPage":33,"pdfPage":51,"alt":"Diagram of a myelinated axon with action potentials traveling between nodes of Ranvier.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":490,"height":594,"source":"Figure excerpt cropped from user-supplied Biological Psychology, 14th ed., PDF","cropPdfPoints":[72,70,317,367],"status":"figure number and printed source page verified against original PDF"}]},{"id":"bp14-m2-1","chapterId":"bp14-ch02","moduleId":"bp14-m2-1","moduleNumber":"2.1","title":"The Concept of the Synapse","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":40,"printedEnd":47,"pdfStart":58,"pdfEnd":65,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Synapses are junctions at which one neuron influences another. Sherrington used reflex behavior to infer that signals can be delayed, combined, or inhibited as they pass through neural circuits."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Temporal summation combines signals across time, while spatial summation combines inputs from different places. Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials jointly influence whether a neuron fires. Focus on the distinction between excitation and inhibition."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-1","text":"The synapse is a decision point"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Signals do not pass freely between all neurons. At a synapse, one cell changes the likelihood that another will become active. Studies of reflexes revealed delays, inhibition, and ways in which several inputs combine. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) moves the receiving cell toward threshold; an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) generally moves it away from threshold or counters excitatory input. Neither is itself the same thing as an action potential. The postsynaptic neuron integrates many changing signals before it fires."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-2","text":"Temporal versus spatial summation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Temporal summation occurs when successive signals from one input arrive close enough together to accumulate before the membrane returns to its earlier state. Spatial summation occurs when inputs at several different locations on a neuron overlap in time. Both matter because single inputs are often too small to trigger an action potential. Whether a neuron fires depends on the size, timing, location, and sign of the incoming postsynaptic potentials rather than on one simple 'on' command."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-3","text":"What inhibition actually does"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Inhibition is an active part of neural computation. An inhibitory input may hyperpolarize a membrane or make it harder for excitation to move the cell toward threshold. Circuits use inhibition to suppress competing actions, sharpen responses, and coordinate sequences. Because neurons receive excitatory and inhibitory signals together, the net effect cannot be predicted by counting excitatory inputs alone. Position on the neuron and the timing of each input influence the outcome."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-4","text":"A useful reasoning model"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Imagine a neuron as continually adding and subtracting influences while deciding whether its membrane at the trigger region reaches threshold. Excitation raises the chance of firing; inhibition lowers it; repeated or simultaneous inputs can add together. This metaphor is useful but should not imply consciousness or deliberation within a single cell. It captures the practical idea that information processing begins at the level of circuits and synaptic integration, long before it looks like a thought or action."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h01","text":"Properties of Synapses"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington based his conclusions on studies of reflexes , automatic muscular responses to stimuli.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In a leg flexion reflex, a sensory neuron excites a second neuron, which in turn excites a motor neuron, which excites a muscle, as in Figure 2.1.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If neurons are separate from one another, as Ramon y Cajal had demonstrated, a reflex must require communication between neurons, and therefore, measurements of reflexes might reveal the properties of their communication.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington strapped a dog into a harness and pinched one of the dog’s feet.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After a fraction of a second, the dog flexed (raised) the pinched leg and extended the other legs.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington found the same reflexive movements after he made a cut that disconnected the spinal cord from the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In an intact animal, messages descending from the brain modify the reflexes, making them stronger at some times and weaker at others.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h02","text":"Speed of a Reflex and Delayed Transmission at the Synapse"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When Sherrington pinched a dog’s foot, the dog flexed that leg after a short delay.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During the delay, an impulse had to travel up an axon from the skin receptor to the spinal cord, and then an impulse had to travel back down the leg to a muscle.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington measured the distance that the impulse traveled from skin to spinal cord to muscle, and then he calculated the speed at which the impulse traveled.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast, previous research had measured action potential velocities along sensory or motor nerves at about 40 m/s.","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington concluded that some process must be slowing conduction through the reflex, and he inferred that the delay occurs where one neuron communicates with another (Figure 2.2).","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h03","text":"Temporal Summation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The neuron delivering transmission is the presynaptic neuron , and the one receiving it is the postsynaptic neuron .","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington proposed that although a single subthreshold excitation in the postsynaptic neuron decays over time, it combines with a second excitation that follows quickly.","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"With a rapid succession of pinches, each adds its effect to what remained from the previous ones, until the combination exceeds the threshold of the postsynaptic neuron, producing an action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Decades later, Sherrington’s former student, John Eccles , attached microelectrodes to stimulate axons of presynaptic neurons while he recorded from the","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A graded depolarization is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) , which results from a sodium ions entering the neuron.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When Eccles produced two EPSPs within a short time, the second EPSP added to what was left of the first one (point 2 in Figure 2.3), producing temporal summation.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h04","text":"Spatial Summation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington also found that synapses have the property of spatial summation —summation over space.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This time, instead of pinching one point twice, he pinched two points at once.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington concluded that pinching two points activated sensory neurons whose axons converged","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Excitation from either sensory axon excited that spinal neuron, and a combination of excitations exceeded the threshold to produce an action potential (point 4 in Figure 2.3).","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Again, Eccles confirmed Sherrington’s inference, demonstrating that EPSPs from several axons summate their effects on a postsynaptic cell (Figure 2.4).","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Temporal summation and spatial summation occur together when a neuron receives input from several axons in succession.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h05","text":"Inhibitory Synapses"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A dog raising one leg needs to extend the other legs to maintain balance.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The dog also relaxed the extensor muscles of the stimulated leg and the flexor muscles of the other legs.","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The interneuron also sends messages to inhibit the extensor muscles in that leg and the flexor muscles of the three other legs.","sourcePrintedPage":43,"sourcePdfPage":61,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most neurons have a spontaneous firing rate , a periodic production of action potentials even without synaptic input.","sourcePrintedPage":43,"sourcePdfPage":61,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In such cases, the EPSPs increase the frequency of action potentials above the spontaneous rate, whereas IPSPs decrease it.","sourcePrintedPage":43,"sourcePdfPage":61,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For a neuron with a spontaneous firing rate of 10 action potentials per second, a stream of EPSPs might increase the rate to 15 or more, whereas a preponderance of IPSPs might decrease it to 5 or fewer.","sourcePrintedPage":43,"sourcePdfPage":61,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"among neurons, but for a given neuron, it stays within a narrow range .","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h06","text":"Relationship among EPSP, IPSP, and Action Potentials"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington’s work opened the way to exploring the wiring diagram of the nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When neuron 1 excites neuron 3, it also excites neuron 2, which inhibits neuron 3.","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The excitatory message reaches neuron 3 faster because it goes through just one synapse instead of two.","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The result is a burst of excitation (EPSP) in neuron 3, which quickly slows or stops.","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The axon from either cell A or cell B stimulates cell X with 1 1 unit.","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If the threshold of cell X is 1 1, then cell X responds to “A or B.” If the threshold is 1 2, then cell X responds to","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h07","text":"In Closing: The Neuron as Decision Maker"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The EPSPs and IPSPs reaching a neuron at a given moment compete with one another.","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The combined effect of EPSPs and IPSPs determines whether or not the postsynaptic cell fires an action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, do not imagine that any single neuron decides what you will eat for breakfast.","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, some synapses produce fast, brief effects, and others produce slow, long-lasting effects.","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The effect of two synapses at the same time can be more than double the effect of either one, or less than double .","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Also, many neurons in the brain change their properties from one context to another.","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An experimenter finds that stimulating neuron X causes an action potential in neuron Z after a short delay.","sourcePrintedPage":46,"sourcePdfPage":64,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"In fact, the movements were more consistent after he separated the spinal cord from the brain.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sherrington observed several properties of reflexes that suggest special processes at the junctions between neurons: (1) Reflexes are slower than conduction along an axon.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58},{"type":"bullet","text":"He called this phenomenon temporal summation, meaning summation over time.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59},{"type":"bullet","text":"A light pinch of the dog’s foot did not evoke a reflex, but a few rapidly repeated pinches did.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59},{"type":"bullet","text":"Depending on the charge he delivered through the microelectrode, Eccles recorded a slight depolarization of the membrane of the postsynaptic cell (point 1 in Figure 2.3) or a slight hyperpolarization (point 5).","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60},{"type":"bullet","text":"Unlike action potentials, which are always depolarizations, graded potentials may be either depolarizations (excitatory) or hyperpolarizations (inhibitory), and they decay over both time and distance.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60},{"type":"bullet","text":"He again began with a pinch too weak to elicit a reflex.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60},{"type":"bullet","text":"Although neither pinch alone produced a reflex, together they did.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60},{"type":"bullet","text":"When Sherrington vigorously pinched a dog’s foot, the flexor muscles of that leg contracted, and so did the extensor muscles of the other three legs.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":42,"sourcePdfPage":60},{"type":"bullet","text":"At these synapses, input from an axon hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic cell, moving the cell’s charge farther from the threshold and decreasing the probability of an action potential (point 5 in Figure 2.3).","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":43,"sourcePdfPage":61},{"type":"bullet","text":"Today, we take for granted the concept of inhibition, but at Sherrington’s time, the idea was controversial, as no one could imagine a mechanism to accomplish it.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62},{"type":"bullet","text":"Establishing the idea of inhibition was critical not just for neuroscience but for psychology as well.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62},{"type":"bullet","text":"You can now understand how inhibitory messages can regulate the timing of activity.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":44,"sourcePdfPage":62},{"type":"bullet","text":"Complex behaviors depend on the contributions from a huge network of neurons.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63},{"type":"bullet","text":"“A and B.” Following this same logic, you may be able to imagine other constructions.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63},{"type":"bullet","text":"Many mathematical models of the nervous system are based on connections like these.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":45,"sourcePdfPage":63},{"type":"bullet","text":"When Sherrington measured the reaction time of a reflex (i.e., the delay between stimulus and response), he found that the response occurred faster after a strong stimulus than after a weak one.","headingId":"bp14-m2-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":46,"sourcePdfPage":64},{"type":"bullet","text":"Suppose neuron X has a synapse onto neuron Y, which has a synapse onto
